extracted.intended_audience: ARIPO patent examiners, search examiners, patent attorneys/agents and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on determining whether a patent application complies with the requirement of unity of invention (single invention or a group linked by a single general inventive concept), including how to identify special technical features, permitted claim combinations, and examiner procedures during search and substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An ARIPO application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept (Section 2(9)(a), Rule 7(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second alternative permits a plurality of independent claims in the same or different categories provided they comply with the single general inventive concept requirement. The single general inventive concept must link claims in the various categories; mere use of phrases like 'specially adapted' does not necessarily imply unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special technical features — definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Special technical features are the particular technical feature(s) in a claim that define the contribution the claimed invention as a whole makes over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the special technical features of each invention, then determine whether a technical relationship exists between inventions that involves these special technical features. Corresponding (not necessarily identical) special technical features across claims can provide the required link (e.g., metal spring vs rubber block providing resilience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible combinations of claims (forms of claiming linked inventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain combinations of independent claims in different categories may be included in one application if they belong to a single general inventive concept (examples include product + process for manufacture + use; process + apparatus designed for process; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidelines list six forms (i)-(vi) illustrating allowable combinations: multiple independent claims of same category; product + process specially adapted to manufacture it; product + use; product+process+use; product+process+apparatus specifically designed for the process; process+apparatus specifically designed for the process. These examples are not exhaustive — other combinations are permissible if they share a single general inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Specially adapted' / 'specifically designed' does not automatically create unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions like 'specially adapted' or 'specifically designed' in claims do not necessarily imply a single general inventive concept linking claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a process to be 'specially adapted' it must actually result in the claimed product (i.e., be suited to making the claimed product accessible). For an apparatus to be 'specifically designed' it must be suitable for carrying out the process and the contribution it makes over the prior art should correspond to that made by the process. It is irrelevant whether the apparatus could be used for other processes or the process by other apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity for intermediate and final products
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity may be present between intermediate and final products when they (i) share the same essential structural element (basic chemical structures the same or intermediate incorporates essential element), and (ii) are technically closely interrelated (final product manufactured directly from intermediate or separated by a small number of intermediates containing the same essential element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity can exist even when structures are unknown (e.g., intermediate known, final unknown) provided sufficient evidence shows technical interrelation. Different intermediates used in different processes may be claimed provided they have the same essential structural element. Intermediates separated by a non‑new intermediate breaks unity. Families of intermediates/final products should correspond compound-for-compound where applicable; family congruence need not be absolute. Other activities/effects of intermediates do not necessarily prejudice unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives and unity within single claims (including Markush groupings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative forms of an invention may be claimed in plural independent claims or within a single claim; the same unity criteria apply and lack of unity may exist within a single claim. For Markush groupings unity exists if the alternatives are of a similar nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical Markush groupings, alternatives are 'similar' if (i) all alternatives share a common property or activity, and (ii) a common structure is present (a significant structural element shared) or all alternatives belong to a recognized class of compounds expected to behave similarly. A small shared portion can be sufficient if it is structurally distinctive in view of the prior art. If at least one Markush alternative is not novel, unity should be reconsidered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition of unconnected features does not create lack of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unity does not arise merely because a claim contains a number of individual features that do not present a technical interrelationship (i.e., mere juxtaposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only where features form a technical combination (interrelated) should unity be considered lacking; simple listing of unrelated features in one claim is not, by itself, a unity objection trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of unity a priori vs a posteriori
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unity may be apparent a priori (before considering prior art) or only apparent a posteriori (after taking prior art into account).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A priori lack of unity arises when inventions obviously have no same or corresponding technical feature (e.g., herbicide vs mower). A posteriori lack of unity can arise when prior art shows lack of novelty or inventive step in an independent claim, leaving dependent claims without a common inventive concept; examiners must reassess unity in such situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's practical approach and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should avoid narrow, literal or academic approaches to unity; consider the practical degree of interdependence of alternatives in relation to the state of the art revealed by the search report and give the benefit of doubt to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not raise or persist in unity objections where unnecessary (especially if no further search is required). If common matter of independent claims is well known and remaining subject-matter differs with no unifying novel concept, objection is justified. Each case should be considered on its merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of dependent claims with respect to unity
rubrics_metrics.description: No objection of lack of unity a priori is justified between a dependent claim and the claim on which it depends merely because they share the general concept of the independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the independent claim is found not patentable, examiners must reconsider whether dependent claims still share an inventive link. Special technical features of dependent claims may not correspond across different dependents, so reassessment is necessary when the parent is non‑patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search Examiner actions on lack of unity during search
rubrics_metrics.description: Search Examiners may note and report lack of unity by drawing up a partial search report based on those parts of the application relating to the first‑mentioned invention; they may not refuse for lack of unity or require claim limitation but must inform applicant of additional search fees if they wish other inventions searched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may pay further search fees within a stipulated period to have other inventions covered in the search report. The Search Examiner's partial search report records the lack-of-unity findings for later substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive Examiner responsibilities when lack of unity arises
rubrics_metrics.description: Final responsibility for deciding whether the application meets unity rests with the Substantive Examiner, who will generally follow the search opinion but must consider applicant arguments and may order further search or require deletion/limitation of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant paid further fees and requested refund, Substantive Examiner will order refund where appropriate. If applicant did not seek searches of other inventions, the application proceeds on the searched invention. Examiner should invite applicant to elect which invention prosecution should proceed on and may require excision/amendment or divisional filings for other inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required applicant actions when lack of unity is found
rubrics_metrics.description: When unity is found to be lacking, applicant should be required to limit claims to overcome the objection; excision or amendment of description parts may also be necessary and divisional applications may be filed to cover removed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should request the applicant to elect an invention for prosecution and to limit the application accordingly; divisional applications are the route to pursue excised inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of examination — focus on substantive content and special technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine unity, examine whether substantive contents of the technical solutions in the claims belong to a single general inventive concept by checking for same or corresponding special technical features that make the claimed inventions technically interrelated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is made primarily on the basis of claims, referring to description/drawings if necessary. The order or form of claims does not affect unity determination. Generally consider unity among independent claims; normally do not object between independent and its dependent claims, except where a dependent is in form but actually independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of unity determination (before or after search)
rubrics_metrics.description: For some applications unity can be decided before search (when inventions obviously lack unity), but for many applications determination requires consideration of prior art and can only be made after search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a first independent claim is denied novelty/inventive step after search, re‑determine whether the remaining independent claims belong to a single general inventive concept. Obvious lack of unity (no same/corresponding technical features or only customary means) can be determined pre-search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step approach to examining unity (practical procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recommended approach when unity is not obviously lacking: (1) compare first invention with relevant prior art to identify its special technical feature; (2) determine whether the second invention contains same or corresponding special technical features; (3) conclude unity if such same/corresponding features exist, otherwise conclude lack of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stepwise method underlies the examiner examples and practical assessments; it emphasizes identification of contribution over prior art as the linchpin for interrelation between claimed inventions.
